name: Bronze
lede: Bronze is the brown of the metal alloy of copper and tin: darker and duller than gold, and the name of an age.

sections.title: A metal's name, a brown's swatch
sections.body:
*Bronze* names an alloy of copper first, and a color second. Paterson's dictionary defines the color as the brilliant brown of the metal, and traces the word to Brindisi, the Italian town [1]. Clair's list of color names gives a plainer gloss: the color of the metal, darker and duller than gold [2].

The swatch on this page is not shiny. #756033 is a dark olive-brown, filed by the ISCC-NBS names of 1955 as a moderate yellowish brown, and it traces back to Ridgway's atlas of 1912 and the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 [6]. A screen cannot show the gleam that makes metal read as metal. What remains is the flat brown a bronze has when the highlights are taken away.

That gap between a metal and its flat swatch matters for the name's use in fashion too. In the 1880s Clair notes "art bronze" among the combinations offered with heliotrope, alongside canary yellow, eucalyptus green and peacock blue [3]. Paterson defines "antique bronze" separately, as a color imitating very old objects [1].

sections.title: From alloy to paint
sections.body:
Bronze reached the painter's shop as a metal powder. The Pigment Compendium records that metallic bronze of a grey color was found on three paintings by Perugino, with an alloy of tin to copper in the ratio 1:2, which appears grey when ground dry [14]. The same entry notes brass powders as metallic pigments on Japanese artifacts [14].

"Bronzing" became a trade term: in Paterson's definition it is a pigment added in manufacturing paint to give a metallic lustre, and also the process of dusting or leafing a surface with imitation gold [1]. The word then spread to other metals: the Compendium observes that "aluminium bronze powder" took its name by association with powders made from copper alloys, even though aluminium powder was probably available only from the mid-nineteenth century [15].

There was also a paint called bronze green, and the books disagree about what it was. Salter in 1869 described it as a kind of Prussian green, a dull blue-black that looks like greenish-black with a coppery cast in deep washes [16]. Linke and Adam in 1913 treat it as a trade name for cinnabar green or chrome green, and Heaton in 1928 as a variety of Brunswick green [16]. Winsor and Newton's 1938 water-color of the name was a mixed chrome green [16]. The name stayed the same while the recipe changed; the modern color is [[bronze-green]].

A sheen can be called bronze without any metal in it. Coles notes that Prussian blue, as a concentrated pigment, has a bronze sheen [4]. That sheen belongs to the surface of the dense pigment, not to its hue [4].

sections.title: The Bronze Age and its colors
sections.body:
The metal gave a whole era its name, and color was entangled with it. Ball suggests that a love of color ushered in the Bronze Age: the kilns built to fire blue-glazed faience may have led the way to copper smelting [5]. He presents this as a plausible inference, not a documented chain of events. What is firmer is that [[egyptian-blue]], which he calls the oldest synthetic pigment, is a Bronze Age blue [5].

Gage notes that blues of this kind appear in the Bronze Age wall paintings of Thera, Knossos and Mycenae [7]. A passage from the *Odyssey* that Gage quotes pictures a palace whose walls are bronze, topped with blue enamel tiles [7]. In the ancient imagination, the metal and the blue went together.

Bronze does not stay brown. Paterson notes that bronze sculpture left to the weather oxidizes, develops a patina of verdigris and turns green [1]. Pastoureau shows a Roman imperial bronze coin whose green patina comes from the same oxidation [8]. The green of an old statue is time's work, not the founder's.

A myth lives in this neighborhood. In the nineteenth century Gladstone argued that Greek poetry's color words, which describe the sea as bronze-colored rather than blue or green, showed that the Greeks could hardly see blue [9]. That is a myth. Pastoureau reports the argument and sets it aside: what the poems show is how the Greeks used color words, not what their eyes could do [9].

sections.title: Gold's duller cousin
sections.body:
For centuries bronze has stood in for gold where gold was too costly or too showy. Pastoureau describes a period in which yellow lost its prestige, and in the furnishings of wealthy homes burnished bronzes replaced the gold and gilding of earlier times [10]. Bronze offered the warmth of a metal with less of its claim to rank.

Pearls come in bronze as well. Finlay lists bronze among the colors of pearls, between apricot and pink [11]. In a quite different meaning, to *bronze* is to tan, a verb Paterson defines for skin that is browned by the sun or by cosmetics [1]. Pastoureau notes that the fashion for a bronzed tan flipped: it became vulgar once everyone could have it, and fear of cancer finished the job [12].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Bronze is among the most common named colors in our painting archive. It appears in 4,535 of 23,781 paintings, 19.07 per cent, which is more common than 96 per cent of the named colors; the within-painting lens finds it in 2,407 [13]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 35 per cent of those 2,407 [13].

It peaks in the 1600s: it is found in 706 of the 6,394 paintings we have from that century, 11.0 per cent, or 1.1 times the rate of the same museums' baseline [13]. The most devoted painter is Fritz Thomsen, in 8 of his 18 works here, 4.8 times the baseline; Salomon van Ruysdael, Paulus Potter, George Catlin and Juan Carreño de Miranda follow [13]. These are the browns of dark, varnished landscapes and animal pictures, not of metal.

The first dated match is a painting from the year 799, but the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first [13]. The name's earliest record in our sources is 1912, so the match is a look-alike brown in an aged photograph, not proof of the pigment or dye [13]. In printed English the color word peaks in the 1930s, and rose fastest in the 1920s (Google Books, adjective use only) [13].
